stories.notes: Live preview across GO, UP, MX is a complex cross-platform feature with empty acceptance criteria and no existing spec. openspec must elaborate requirements first; speckit then hardens with testability, security (untrusted content rendering), and edge cases.

agentContributions.notes: Story requests a new Live Preview capability for Contentstack CMS — novel, not a defect. The attachment point is useContent, the single hook through which all 236+ components fetch content. Live preview must plug into this layer (or its provider) to deliver real-time/draft content to the preview surface. Downstream components (ContentstackLink, ContentstackImage, ContentstackTable, etc.) consume useContent and should require no individual changes. Acceptance criteria were empty; VCs derived solely from the description.

Openspec provided empty acceptanceCriteria with useful architectural context: the attachment point is useContent, downstream components (236+) should require no individual changes, and the three codebases (gotransit, upexpress, metrolinx) all share the same relevant files. I derived all 13 ACs from that context plus the story title and description. Key areas covered: (1) core preview/non-preview behavior (AC-1, AC-2), (2) real-time update delivery (AC-3, AC-11), (3) downstream component transparency (AC-4, AC-8, AC-12), (4) error handling/fallback (AC-5, AC-6), (5) security/leakage prevention (AC-7), (6) accessibility parity (AC-9), (7) multi-site parity (AC-10), (8) session lifecycle (AC-13). I could not inspect the actual file contents of useContent.ts, contentstack.ts, contentCard.ts, or ContentstackLink.tsx — if those files reveal existing preview infrastructure, preview-parameter conventions, or specific Contentstack SDK methods already in use, some ACs may need tightening (e.g., AC-7's 'preview parameters' wording may need to match the actual query-string or header convention the codebase uses).

coordinatorReview.reviewNotes: Both agents added meaningful, non-overlapping value. openspec provided architectural grounding — identifying useContent as the sole attachment point, confirming downstream components (236+) need no individual changes, and classifying the story as a novel feature rather than a defect. speckit then translated that architectural context into 13 concrete ACs spanning core behavior, real-time updates, downstream transparency, error handling, security/leakage prevention, accessibility parity, multi-site parity, and session lifecycle. The division of labor is clean: openspec answered 'where and how,' speckit answered 'what must be true.' However, speckit explicitly flagged that it could not inspect actual file contents (useContent.ts, contentstack.ts, contentCard.ts, ContentstackLink.tsx), meaning several ACs — particularly AC-7's 'preview parameters' wording — may not align with real codebase conventions or existing preview infrastructure. Given the feature's complexity (live preview across three codebases, untrusted content rendering, real-time delivery), this unverified-against-codebase gap is a material risk. Human review should validate ACs against actual source files before implementation begins.
